title: Fog supplies much of the water in Namibia's coastal dunes
body: In the Namib Sand Sea, fog is the main source of water. It reaches extensive dune fields beside the Atlantic, where animals and plants live with very little rainfall.
takeaway: A place can receive little rain and still have a recurring supply of moisture from the sea.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Namib Sand Sea (2013)
visual: fog rolling in from the Atlantic across tall desert dunes

title: Rainforest grows on sand on Australia's largest sand island
body: Off Queensland, K'gari is about 122 km long. Tall rainforest grows on its coastal dunes, and the island has freshwater lakes perched above the surrounding water table.
takeaway: Sand can support a forest where water and nutrients accumulate long enough for trees to take hold.
visual: a tall rainforest canopy just beyond a crest of pale coastal sand

title: Iguazu Falls straddles two countries across about 2.7 km
body: The Iguazu River drops about 80 metres over a basalt edge between Argentina and Brazil. Its semicircular brink divides into many cascades as the water passes around islands and ledges.
takeaway: The shared falls make the same river landscape a conservation responsibility on both sides of the border.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Iguazu and Iguacu National Parks
visual: a broad curving line of cascades pouring into a misty gorge

title: The sea flooded a landscape of limestone towers in Vietnam
body: Ha Long Bay and the neighbouring Cat Ba Archipelago include 1,133 islands and islets within their World Heritage boundary. Their steep limestone towers are part of a landscape shaped by the erosion of soluble rock and later invaded by the sea.
takeaway: Some features that look like islands from a boat began as part of a landscape on land.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ha Long Bay and Cat Ba Archipelago
visual: steep limestone pillars rising from still water in Ha Long Bay
